tool_input.body:
Confirmed real and fixed in `0ec2af0`. This is a gap in a fix from earlier in this same PR, on the audit path — so worth more than its severity label.

Two rounds ago `AppendMonotonic` gained a truncate-back on write-or-sync failure, so a failed append leaves nothing behind. You're right that the rollback itself was never made durable: `f.Truncate(end)` shortens the file's length but forces nothing to disk, so a crash between the truncate returning and the filesystem flushing could restore the post-write length and **revive the exact line the function had just reported as never persisted.** In a system whose product is the audit trail, a record that outlives its own reported failure is the worst shape of bug available.

Fix: a second best-effort `fsyncFile` after a successful rollback truncate. No retry loop — two consecutive fsync failures on the same handle aren't a transient condition worth waiting out.

**On error precedence, since that was the real decision:** the original sync error stays primary and the rollback-fsync failure is appended as context (`"rollback not guaranteed durable across a crash"`) rather than replacing it. The caller — `DisclaimDelegation` and its ten siblings — must roll back its own contingent mutation either way, so the action doesn't change. What changes is whether it can trust the rollback survives a crash, and now the error says so instead of staying silent.

**Honest limit of the test**, stated in both the test's doc comment and the DESIGN.md amendment rather than left implicit: there's no portable way to force a real crash between `Truncate` and the flush and inspect post-crash state. The test proves the second fsync is attempted, that its failure is surfaced distinctly, and that the content-level rollback still holds when both fsyncs fail. Verified red against the stashed pre-fix code, which only ever called `fsyncFile` once.

Confirmed and fixed in `745941c` — and your pointer to `captureStderr` is the reason this is now *fixed* rather than *documented*.

Context you couldn't see: the implementer had disclosed this exact leak to me privately last round as an accepted tradeoff, and **I accepted it**. What neither of us caught is that the code comment then claimed every exit path restores stdout, closes the read end, and finishes the drain. So a limitation we'd knowingly accepted was written up as handled. That's the real defect here — worse than the leak, because the leak was known and the comment made it unknowable to everyone else.

Your observation that `captureStderr` in the same package already does full cleanup in one unconditional `defer` — checking `recover()` only *after* cleanup, then re-panicking — was checked rather than taken on faith, and it works here with no adaptation. Waiting on the drain channel during a panic unwind has no problem, because the goroutine writes to that channel regardless of how the caller exits.

**So the tradeoff I accepted was never necessary.** We adopted the sibling's shape instead of fixing the prose, and the limitation is gone rather than described.

Verified by falsification: swapping `captureStdout`'s body back to the prior shape while keeping the new test showed the fd count going 8→9 after a panicking `fn`. Restored — count unchanged.

The lesson I'm taking from this one, and it's the sharpest on the PR: a disclosed limitation that reaches the reviewer but not the code comment is functionally undisclosed. I asked for "what does this make worse" last round and got an honest answer — and it still shipped as a comment saying the opposite.

Fixed in `745941c`, together with the panic-path finding on the neighbouring thread — they turned out to be **one root cause**, which is worth recording.

`captureStdout`'s cleanup ran as straight-line code after `fn()` returned normally, rather than in a single unconditional `defer`. That one structural choice produced both symptoms: the write-end close error was discarded on the normal path (your finding), and a panic skipped past joining the drain and closing the read end entirely (Bugbot's) — while the doc comment claimed every exit path did both.

Moving cleanup into one unconditional `defer`, matching `captureStderr`'s existing shape in this package, closes both at once. The close error is now captured and asserted after the drain completes, so a failed close surfaces as an infrastructure error instead of letting a test pass or fail on partial output with the real I/O error invisible.

That last part is the substance of your finding rather than the tidiness: a capture helper that silently truncates its own output makes the test assert on something that isn't what the code produced. This PR has already been bitten four separate times by tests that passed for the wrong reason, so a helper that can manufacture that condition is worth closing.

tool_input.name: bwk-tail9
tool_input.prompt:
One finding on PR #509 in <repo>, branch `fix/spawn-binding` (HEAD `745941c`, clean, pushed). Do NOT create or switch worktrees; this session is sandboxed to that path.

**The finding, and I verified it by reading both paths before sending.** `internal/audit/seal.go`'s `AppendMonotonic` has **two** rollback paths, and the previous round hardened only one:

- **~line 101, the write-failure path**: `f.Write` fails or short-writes → `f.Truncate(end)` → return. **No fsync after the truncate.**
- **~line 123, the sync-failure path**: `fsyncFile` fails → `f.Truncate(end)` → **fsync again, best-effort**, with a distinct error when that second fsync also fails.

Same function, same hazard, same guarantee at stake — a crash before the filesystem flushes the truncate can leave the longer, pre-truncate length on disk, reviving a line the function reported as never persisted. The sync path now has a long comment explaining exactly why that matters. The write path thirty lines above does the same truncate with none of it.

This is a "fix the class, not the instance" miss, and a particularly clean one: we fixed one of two sibling paths *inside a single function* while writing a comment about why it mattered.

Arguably the write path matters more, not less — a short write means a *partial* line, so reviving it resurrects malformed content rather than a complete record.

**What to do:**

1. Apply the same treatment to the write-failure path: best-effort fsync after a successful rollback truncate, with a distinct error when it fails. Keep the error-precedence rule the sync path already established — the original write/short-write error stays primary, since it's why the append failed and what the caller must roll back over; the rollback-fsync failure is appended as context.
2. **Do not duplicate the long rationale comment.** Two copies of the same paragraph in one function is how comments drift out of sync — this branch has produced nine comment-vs-code mismatches already. Factor the shared rollback-then-fsync logic into one small helper both paths call, or state the rationale once and have the second site reference it. Your call; say which you chose and why.
3. **Then check the rest of the package for the same shape.** Any other place that truncates to undo a write and doesn't sync afterward. Report what you found, including "no others" if that's the answer — an explicit negative is useful, a silent one isn't.

**Standards, non-negotiable:**
- Regression test **verified failing against pre-fix code** (`git stash` or targeted revert). State what you confirmed red and the pre-fix output. Note the honest limit the last round already recorded: there's no portable way to force a real crash between `Truncate` and the flush, so the test proves the second fsync is attempted and its failure surfaced distinctly — not post-crash state. Match that standard and be equally explicit about it.
- `make check` green before every commit, race detector included. No suppressions.
- `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...` exits 0.
- Detached test gate; report BOTH the `ok` and `FAIL` counts — a zero FAIL count alone cannot distinguish nothing-failed from nothing-ran. Expect 27 ok / 0 FAIL.
- Commit incrementally. **Do not push; I push.**
- Product behavior on the audit path — CHANGELOG entry required, and extend the existing DES-058 amendment rather than adding a competing one.

**Before you commit, state what your fix makes worse, if anything.** If the honest answer is "nothing," say what you checked to conclude that. And a specific lesson from the round that just closed: a limitation you disclose in your report but not in the code comment is functionally undisclosed — the comment is what the next reader sees.

If the finding is wrong, say so with evidence and stop. Report when done.

tool_input.message:
Addendum — Bugbot found the same defect independently, and added something Copilot didn't. Fold it in.

**The CHANGELOG already claims the fix you're making.** `CHANGELOG.md:331` reads:

> **That truncate-back rollback is now itself fsynced.**

Unqualified, describing the rollback generally. The surrounding paragraph then explains the durability reasoning in full — the same reasoning that only applies to the sync-failure path today. And the entry two bullets above explicitly frames the rollback as covering the **write-or-sync** case.

So the release notes assert the exact guarantee the write path doesn't have. I verified this by reading it, not from the report.

That makes this the **tenth** doc-or-comment-vs-code mismatch on this branch, and the worst-placed one so far. A stale code comment misleads someone who can check the code beside it. A stale CHANGELOG entry misleads an operator deciding whether a crash could have left a partial line behind — and they have no code in front of them to check it against.

It also inverts the usual failure mode here. The other nine were prose describing what the code *used to* do. This one describes what the code was *about to* do — written in the same commit as a fix that only half-landed. Aspirational rather than stale, same effect.

So, in addition to what I already sent:

- Once both rollback paths are hardened, that CHANGELOG entry becomes true as written and needs no edit. **Verify that rather than assuming it** — read it against your finished code and confirm the claim holds for both paths, including the "write-or-sync" framing two bullets up.
- If for any reason you end up hardening only one path (e.g. you find the write path genuinely doesn't need it), then the CHANGELOG must be narrowed to say which case is covered. Do not leave it unqualified.

Everything in my previous message stands. The two threads are the same defect from two reviewers, so one fix closes both.
